message.reasoning:
I need to make a decision in Monopoly.

I am p2 with $2111 and a pink monopoly of three hotels. The opponent has $216 and hotels on light blues plus Park Place and Boardwalk. I have two get-out-of-jail cards.

All other properties are mortgaged. Pennsylvania Avenue is owned by p1 but mortgaged, so no rent is due. The options are end_turn, propose_trade, unmortgage a railroad or Tennessee Avenue, or sell hotels on the pink monopoly. The prior strategy avoids unmortgaging, trading Tennessee Avenue, selling hotels, and spending get-out-of-jail cards.

Rolling 3 from Pennsylvania Avenue lands on Park Place with a hotel. Rolling 5 lands on Boardwalk with a hotel. Both spaces are heavily rented.

Boardwalk hotel rent is $2000, leaving $111 cash. Park Place hotel rent is $1500, leaving $611. Both are affordable with current cash. Selling hotels before the roll would reduce the income drain. The timing of this post-turn decision relative to the dice roll is unclear.

The turn flow is now clearer. Dice rolls and movement happen before post-turn actions. Recent events lack dice roll logs, suggesting this may be a post-turn decision after the move has already occurred. I must have moved from Illinois to Pennsylvania Avenue.

The move from Illinois to Pennsylvania Avenue was a roll of 10. The opponent will act next, then I will roll again from Pennsylvania Avenue.

Unmortgaging the Pennsylvania Railroad costs $110 against a $100 mortgage value, so it shrinks the cash cushion with no set benefit. Unmortgaging Tennessee Avenue would complete the orange set for the opponent, since they already own St. James Place, New York Avenue, and the other orange properties.

The opponent has $216 and could use it to unmortgage and build. They already hold hotels on the most dangerous sets. The orange set would remain mortgaged even if completed.

Unmortgaging the Pennsylvania Railroad would leave $2001, barely enough to cover Boardwalk hotel rent of $2000. That one-dollar gap is too risky.

Unmortgaging Tennessee Avenue would leave $2012, enough to cover Boardwalk, but it would only yield a base rent of $14 with no set benefit. Trading with the opponent seems unpromising because they will not give up their dark blue hotels or light blue properties.

I considered offering cash for one of the opponent's dark blue hotels. They would never accept breaking their monopoly without an enormous price. Even with all $2111, I would be broke and they would still have cash to spend.

A trade for Boardwalk would force the opponent to sell their Park Place hotel first. Hotels require a set monopoly, so removing one property from the dark blue set would destroy the hotel. The trade system might also reject trading properties that still have buildings on them.

The safest path is to end the turn. Buying mortgaged properties would be useless without completing a set. The next roll from Pennsylvania Avenue risks either a $1500 Park Place hotel or a $2000 Boardwalk hotel, leaving $611 or $111 cash. A roll of four lands on the luxury tax for $100, leaving $2011. All other outcomes are safe.

The opponent is on Atlantic Avenue. Their next roll cannot land on my pink properties, since the minimum forward move from 26 is 28 and my pinks sit at 11, 13, and 14. They would need to go all the way around the board.

The opponent cannot land on my pink properties until they loop around the board. From a position near 30, the pinks sit about 21 spaces ahead, so they would need at least two more turns to reach them.

I must time the race carefully: they need to hit my pink hotels and be forced to sell their dark blue hotels before I land on Boardwalk or Park Place twice.

Pink hotel rents are $750 for St. Charles Place and States Avenue, and $900 for Virginia Avenue.

Their liquidation capacity is limited to $216 in cash plus brown houses sold at half price.

Standard Monopoly rules allow selling a hotel back to four houses for half the hotel cost. Each house costs $50, so two brown houses sell for $50 total. Light blue hotels can be fully liquidated by converting them to four houses and selling those houses at half price.

The opponent can liquidate all buildings for roughly $425, combined with $216 cash to reach about $641. That is still below the $750 pink hotel rent. They would need to sell a dark blue hotel and then a house to cover it.

The strategy is to force the opponent to downgrade a dark blue hotel to three houses. That would drop Boardwalk rent from $2000 to $1400 or $1000, making repeated hits survivable. Selling my own pink hotels would backfire by lowering their rent to four-house levels and weakening my position.

I realized my prior estimates for pink hotel rents were wrong. Standard Monopoly rules set St. Charles Place and States Avenue at $750 per house and $950 with a hotel, while Virginia Avenue is $800 per house and $1000 with a hotel. The earlier figures of $750/$750/$900 appear to be four-house levels or incorrect values.

Turn 227 records a $1700 four-house rent on Boardwalk, confirming standard Monopoly rules apply. The earlier pink hotel rent of $750/$750/$900 is inconsistent with standard tables and likely reflects a four-house level or error. I will use standard Monopoly rent values for all properties.

The earlier $750 pink hotel estimate was a four-house level, not the true hotel rent. Standard Monopoly sets pink hotels at $950/$950/$1000, which is even more profitable for the cash drain. Selling my own hotels would reduce that income. I will not trade with the opponent now; they have no incentive to give up their dark blue hotels or Tennessee Avenue.

No incomplete sets remain to complete. Buying a mortgaged property would not help, since railroads do not create color monopolies and their rent is too low to justify the cash. A generous trade proposal could be rejected, wasting an action, but ending the turn remains the only viable path.

Selling the pink hotels would reduce the cash drain, but I can already afford Boardwalk hotel rent with my current cash. That makes selling them strictly worse unless I expect to hit Boardwalk and another expensive property or draw a favorable Chance card.

A roll of 2 from position 34 lands on a Chance space. Some cards like "go to Boardwalk" or "general repairs" would cost $2000 or $300–$345, which I can afford, but the timing could still leave me short if I hit Boardwalk right after repairs.
